title: How much text at once
question: One word, a verse, a passage or a whole chapter?
lede: People increasingly read Scripture on phones, in short and frequent sessions. Apps answer with verse cards, focus modes, read-along highlighting and even speed readers. Each decides how much of the Bible someone holds in mind at once, from a single word to a whole chapter. The church has read in many measures. An app should help people hear the word, not just get through it.
calling: Choose the unit that helps someone hear the word, not the one that helps them finish.

spectrum.title: From one word to a whole chapter

working_example.situation: Someone has a few minutes before work and opens Mark 4 at the storm on the sea (4:35–41). Every option starts there, in the Berean Standard Bible. Read to the end of the passage, then try to find what Jesus was doing just before.

options.name: One word at a time
options.origin: Borrowed from speed-reading tools such as Spritz and Kindle Word Runner, which flash one word at a time at a chosen speed.
options.makes_easier: No eye movement and no lost place; it can feel fast and very focused for short, familiar text.
options.costs: You cannot glance back, and readers reread 10–15% of the time; comprehension tends to drop. It also turns Scripture into a speed.
options.ask_your_team: Is there any reading in your product that should be faster rather than slower?

options.name: One verse at a time
options.origin: Observed in Glorify, which steps through a short passage one verse per screen with a segmented bar (see the screenshots below).
options.makes_easier: An easy start and a slow pace that suits meditation and memory. Each verse gets the whole screen.
options.costs: The chapter is out of sight, and a lone verse is easy to read or share apart from its setting.
options.ask_your_team: How far is every verse from its context, and how does someone get there?

options.name: One verse in focus
options.origin: Observed in Dwell and Soultime during listening (current verse bright, the rest dimmed or hidden); borrowed from iA Writer’s focus mode and karaoke captions.
options.makes_easier: Attention on one verse with the passage still in view; with audio it keeps reader and narrator together.
options.costs: Dimmed text must stay readable and reachable for screen readers, and moving text needs a pause.
options.ask_your_team: Will the focus follow the reader, the narrator, or both?

options.name: One passage
options.origin: Observed in Glorify’s passage readings (Judges 6:11–16 with its own audio); lectionaries, plans and sermons also assign passages. Titles here are our own.
options.makes_easier: A clear beginning and end, the unit sermons and study guides use, and the neighbouring passages one tap away.
options.costs: Where a passage begins and ends, and what it is called, are editorial decisions. Some readers will want the whole chapter.
options.ask_your_team: Who sets the passage boundaries and titles, and how will readers know?

options.name: Whole chapter
options.origin: A familiar convention in Bible apps and e-books; reader’s editions such as the ESV Reader’s Bible remove numbers and headings for longer reading.
options.makes_easier: The argument and story stay whole; the best fit for reading a book through.
options.costs: Long on a phone, and one verse is harder to hold in mind. Headings and numbers shape the reading as much as they help.
options.ask_your_team: Do your readers mostly read through, or dip in?

takeaways.heading: Phones invite shorter, more selective reading
takeaways.text: Screen reading involves more scanning, keyword spotting and selective reading, and less sustained reading (Liu). Comprehension on screens falls behind paper mainly under time pressure, not when people read at their own pace (Delgado et al.). Dyer found app readers completed more days of a plan, while men understood less than in print. Smaller units fit the sessions; they do not guarantee understanding.

takeaways.heading: One word at a time removes looking back
takeaways.text: Readers look back at earlier words 10–15% of the time, and taking that away tends to reduce comprehension (Rayner et al.). For Scripture, which rewards rereading, it is the weakest fit; it also invites reading as a speed. If you offer it, keep it for short, familiar text, with a rewind.

takeaways.heading: A smaller unit has a long devotional history
takeaways.text: Lectio divina reads a few verses slowly and repeatedly. A verse at a time, or a verse in focus, can support that kind of attention and memorisation, as long as the passage is one tap away. Verse numbers date from 1551; a verse was never meant to stand alone. How a reader moves from one card to the next, in order or in a feed that never ends, is a separate decision.

takeaways.heading: Focus with context is the middle path
takeaways.text: A highlighted verse with the passage dimmed around it keeps attention and context together, and works best with audio: read-along highlighting helped children with dyslexia follow, and karaoke-style subtitles have supported literacy at scale. Let readers choose the window, as Immersive Reader does with one, three or five lines.

takeaways.heading: Checking off verses is a second dimension
takeaways.text: Some apps let readers tick off each verse as read; Dewfall, a small iPhone app, does this and counts verses read toward finishing the Bible. That is not another point between one verse and a whole chapter. It decides what counts as read, and it works at any unit. Like one verse per card, it makes the verse the unit, splitting a passage into separate rows, but the passage stays in view. A tick can help someone keep their own place in a long book. It can also reward getting through over taking in: Dyer found app readers finished more of a plan without understanding more. If you offer it, make the tick a deliberate act, never infer it from opening or scrolling, and let it be undone.

takeaways.heading: Passage and chapter carry the argument
takeaways.text: A passage gives a reading its natural shape, the unit preachers and plans use, but its boundaries and titles are editorial. Reader’s editions such as the ESV Reader’s Bible remove numbers and headings so people read longer and follow the story. Make the longer mode calm and easy to enter, and keep the reader’s place across modes.

use_cases.needs: Headings and boundaries to jump between
Text that follows the voice, with pause

findings.heading: Read aloud, together, and whole
findings.text: Israel heard the law read publicly: “they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight” (Nehemiah 8:8). Paul’s letters were read aloud to whole congregations, “after this letter has been read among you” (Colossians 4:16), and Timothy is told, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture” (1 Timothy 4:13). For most of Christian history, Scripture was heard in continuous portions.

findings.heading: Silent, private reading came later
findings.text: Augustine was struck that Ambrose read with his eyes on the page and his voice silent. Personal reading spread with literacy, printing and vernacular Bibles. A phone continues that private line, and can also reconnect people with reading aloud and together.

findings.heading: Small units for prayer and memory
findings.text: “I have hidden Your word in my heart” (Psalm 119:11). Lectio divina dwells on a few verses read slowly and repeatedly; memorisation works verse by verse. Small units are not a modern shortcut; they have their own devotional history.

findings.heading: Context guards meaning
findings.text: Chapter divisions date from the thirteenth century and verse numbers from 1551. Fee and Stuart’s principle, that a text cannot mean what it could never have meant for its first readers, depends on reading a verse within its passage, book and genre.

findings.heading: Most Bible reading is now on screens
findings.text: Two-thirds of US Bible users access the Bible digitally. YouVersion reports over a billion installs and named Isaiah 41:10 its most engaged-with verse of 2025, the fourth time in six years: much digital engagement happens one verse at a time.

findings.heading: Screen reading is more selective
findings.text: People report more browsing, scanning, keyword spotting and one-time reading on screens, and less concentrated reading (Liu). Hutchings shows Bible apps are designed to train particular reading habits.

findings.heading: Completion is not comprehension
findings.text: In Dyer’s church study, app readers finished about two more days of a ten-day plan than print readers, while men understood less on screen. A unit that is easy to finish may not be the one that is understood.

findings.heading: Normal reading is about 240 words a minute
findings.text: Adults read non-fiction at about 238 words a minute, most between 175 and 300. The storm on the sea takes about a minute to read: short enough for any morning.

findings.heading: Skimming finds, deep reading understands
findings.text: Skimmers jump ahead once a section stops paying off; they catch the main points but understand less. Speed-reading displays remove the looking back that comprehension relies on.

findings.heading: Listening is reading too
findings.text: One study found no difference in comprehension between reading, listening, and doing both. Read-along modes serve people who listen as much as people who read.

findings.heading: Memory grows by recall
findings.text: Students who practised recalling a passage remembered 61% a week later; those who reread it remembered 40%. A verse-at-a-time mode for memorisation should ask, not just show.

findings.heading: Pace matters more than medium
findings.text: Screens fall behind paper mainly when people read under time pressure. Let readers set the pace.

findings.heading: Anything that moves needs a pause
findings.text: Content that moves or updates for more than five seconds needs a way to pause, stop or hide it: auto-advancing verses, read-along and word-by-word display all qualify.

findings.heading: Measure, spacing and size
findings.text: Aim for lines under 80 characters, line spacing of at least 1.5, unjustified text and resizing to 200% without sideways scrolling.

findings.heading: Let readers choose the window
findings.text: Immersive Reader lets people focus on one, three or five lines. Offer the size of the focus as a setting, and respect reduced motion.

which_fits.if: Meditation, prayer or memorising a short passage
which_fits.start_with: One verse at a time, or a verse in focus, with the passage one tap away

which_fits.if: Listening while reading, or readers who lose their place
which_fits.start_with: A verse in focus that follows the audio, with pause and rewind

which_fits.if: A daily reading, devotional or group study
which_fits.start_with: One passage with its reference, neighbours and a way into the chapter

which_fits.if: Reading a book through, narrative or argument
which_fits.start_with: The whole chapter, with an option to hide numbers and headings
Leave single-word display out for Scripture study

pulls_against.title: One verse at a time, and the passage around it
pulls_against.pull: One verse to a card is an easy way in, and the same split hides the verses that give it its meaning.
pulls_against.hold: Make cards a door into the passage: keep the verses around each card one tap away, and let readers move to the whole passage whenever they are ready.

reflection.heading: What attention is for
reflection.text: Mary “sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message” (Luke 10:39), and Jesus said she had chosen the good part. Lectio divina dwells on a few verses slowly; reading a whole letter at once shows its argument. Both are forms of attention, and attention is a form of love.

reflection.heading: Where Christians differ
reflection.text: Devotional traditions favour short passages for meditation and memory. Biblical scholars and many teachers urge reading whole books, warning that verse numbers invite reading sentences apart from their context. Silent private reading, which Augustine found remarkable in Ambrose, is itself a later development beside public reading aloud.

reflection.heading: What follows for design
reflection.text: The question is not which unit is more spiritual, but whether the screen keeps a verse connected to its passage and leaves the reader’s attention free. Design for the reader to finish, put the phone down and live what they read (James 1:22).

voices.source: Albert Borgmann, Technology and the Character of Contemporary Life (1984)
voices.note: contrasted “focal practices” that ask for attention and skill with devices that deliver commodities effortlessly; reading Scripture is a focal practice a device can support or displace.
calls for slow, attentive reading in which the text is taken in, not skimmed.

three_ways.exploitative: A feed, badges and notifications compete with the passage for attention.
three_ways.ethical: Offer focus settings and respect the system’s accessibility preferences.
three_ways.redemptive: Design for the reader to finish and close the app, and measure success by that.

decide.question: What unit of Scripture does this screen ask someone to hold in mind, and how do they reach the rest?
decide.exercise: Ask two people to read Mark 4:35–41 in different modes, then retell it and say what Jesus was doing just before. Time how long it takes each to find the verse before 4:35. Repeat with a screen reader and with reduced motion switched on.

earlier_patterns.title: A bounded passage with a route to wider context
earlier_patterns.summary: Choose the reading unit by the task while keeping its boundaries and context visible.

examples.title: One verse per screen, with a step bar
examples.observed: Captured 28 August 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: Jeremiah 17:5–8 (NIV) is shown one verse at a time: verse 6 sits alone mid-screen under a four-part progress bar, with the reference and an information button above, “Bible version: NIV” below, and text-size and notes buttons at the bottom.
examples.decision: A verse at a time slows reading down and suits meditation on a short passage. The step bar keeps the passage boundary in view; the rest of the chapter is out of sight.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: A single verse isolated during playback
examples.observed: Captured 28 August 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: While audio plays, a focus mode shows only Genesis 1:2 in white over a blurred sunset, under “Genesis · Chapter 1”, with a pause button in the corner.
examples.decision: Isolating the verse being read aloud makes listening and reading one act. Nothing on screen shows what came before or comes next.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: The current verse bright, the rest dimmed
examples.observed: Captured 18 September 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: In Dwell’s Listen view, Genesis 1:2 is in full white while verses 1, 3 and 4 above and below are dimmed, each with its reference underneath. A Listen and Read switch sits at the top and a player shows “Genesis 1 · 31 Verses”.
examples.decision: Focus with the context still visible keeps the place during audio without hiding the passage. Check that dimmed text is still readable and announced by screen readers.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: One passage with its own audio
examples.observed: Captured 18 September 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: The header reads “Judges 6:11-16” with a thin progress line beneath it; the passage scrolls in verse paragraphs above a player at 00:59 of 01:44, with speed and volume controls.
examples.decision: A passage-sized unit gives a daily reading a clear beginning and end. Make the way into the rest of Judges 6 as visible as the close button.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

examples.title: A chapter with section headings and verse ranges
examples.observed: Captured 18 September 2025 · from embedded image metadata
examples.observation: Numbers 1 (Hoffnung für Alle, German) opens with “Vorbereitungen zum Aufbruch nach Kanaan”, a range “(Kapitel 1,1–10,10)” and a section heading, then continuous text with small verse numbers and indented name lists, over a play button and chapter arrows.
examples.decision: Long-form reading with headings keeps the chapter’s structure visible. The headings come from the translation’s editors and could be marked as such.
examples.limits: A still image shows one interface state. Gestures, timing, accessibility, persistence and what happens next were not tested. App version not recorded.

sources.title: Reading behavior in the digital environment
sources.author: Ziming Liu · Journal of Documentation 61(6), 2005
sources.shows: Screen reading involves more browsing, scanning, keyword spotting, one-time and selective reading, and less in-depth, concentrated reading.
sources.application: Expect short, selective sessions; design so a short session can still reach context.
sources.limits: A 2005 survey of readers about their own habits; describes reported behaviour, not comprehension.

sources.title: Don’t throw away your printed books: a meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension
sources.author: Delgado, Vargas, Ackerman and Salmerón · Educational Research Review 25, 2018
sources.shows: Paper outperformed screens for comprehension (g = −0.21), mainly for informational texts and under time pressure; the gap was not significant for self-paced reading.
sources.application: Let people read at their own pace; avoid timers and auto-advance for study.
sources.limits: Studies of general texts, mostly before current phone reading apps; not Scripture.

sources.title: So much to read, so little time: how do we read, and can speed reading help?
sources.author: Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman · Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2016
sources.shows: Readers look back at earlier words 10–15% of the time; removing that ability, as one-word-at-a-time display does, tends to reduce comprehension.
sources.application: Do not use single-word display for study; if offered at all, keep it for short, familiar text with a rewind.
sources.limits: Review of reading research; not specific to devotional reading.

sources.title: The habits and hermeneutics of digital Bible readers
sources.author: John Dyer · Journal of Religion, Media and Digital Culture, 2019 (news summary)
sources.shows: Church members read Jude in print or in an app, then followed a 10-day plan in John: app users completed about two more days of reading; men comprehended less on screen than in print, women about the same.
sources.application: Completion and comprehension can move in different directions; measure both.
sources.limits: Small sample from three Dallas churches; reported through a news summary.

sources.title: How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate
sources.author: Marc Brysbaert · Journal of Memory and Language, 2019 (BPS summary)
sources.shows: Across 190 studies, adults read English non-fiction silently at about 238 words a minute (most between 175 and 300).
sources.application: Estimate reading time honestly; a seven-verse passage takes about a minute, not a commitment.
sources.limits: English readers; slower for children, older adults and second-language readers.

sources.title: Does modality matter? The effects of reading, listening, and dual modality on comprehension
sources.author: Rogowsky, Calhoun and Tallal · SAGE Open, 2016 (as reported by APS)
sources.shows: Found no significant difference in comprehension between reading, listening, and reading while listening.
sources.application: Treat listening as real reading, and let people combine it with text.
sources.limits: One nonfiction text with adult readers; other studies find differences for harder texts.

sources.title: Skim reading by satisficing: evidence from eye tracking
sources.author: Duggan and Payne · University of Bath
sources.shows: Skimmers read until a section stops paying off, then jump ahead; they find important points but understand less overall.
sources.application: Support skimming with headings and clear passage boundaries, and offer a slower mode for understanding.
sources.limits: Expository texts in a lab under time pressure.

sources.title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
sources.author: Roediger and Karpicke · Psychological Science, 2006, as discussed in a later review
sources.shows: Students who practised recalling a passage remembered 61% a week later, against 40% for those who reread it.
sources.application: For memorisation, prompt recall of a verse rather than showing it again.
sources.limits: Prose passages with students; not Scripture memorisation specifically.

sources.title: State of the Bible USA 2025
sources.author: American Bible Society
sources.shows: Two-thirds of US Bible users access the Bible digitally; Bible use rose in 2025.
sources.application: Design for phone reading as the norm, not the exception.
sources.limits: US survey by a Bible society; self-reported.

sources.title: YouVersion announces 2025 Verse of the Year
sources.author: ChurchLeaders, reporting YouVersion
sources.shows: Isaiah 41:10 was the most engaged-with verse of 2025 in an app with over a billion installs; the fourth time in six years.
sources.application: Verse-level engagement dominates large apps; design the route from a verse back into its passage.
sources.limits: Company-reported figures; “engaged with” is YouVersion’s own measure.

sources.title: Augustine, Confessions 6.3, on Ambrose reading silently
sources.author: Translation and commentary at Sententiae Antiquae
sources.shows: Augustine was struck that Ambrose read with his eyes on the page while his voice and tongue were silent.
sources.application: A reminder that private, silent reading is one way of reading Scripture among several; public and aloud is the older.
sources.limits: How unusual silent reading was in antiquity is debated by historians.

sources.title: Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth
sources.author: Zondervan, 4th edition 2014 (quotations listing)
sources.shows: Argues that context and genre govern meaning: a text cannot mean what it could never have meant for its first readers.
sources.application: Never strand a verse without a route to its passage and book.
sources.limits: A widely used evangelical introduction to interpretation; one approach among several.

sources.title: ESV Reader’s Bible
sources.author: Crossway
sources.shows: Removes verse numbers, section headings and footnotes so people read books as continuous text and in longer portions.
sources.application: A long-form mode without numbers is an established print choice; keep a way to find references.
sources.limits: Publisher’s rationale, not a study of its effects.

sources.title: Introduction to lectio divina
sources.author: University of St Andrews, School of Divinity
sources.shows: Lectio divina reads a short passage slowly and repeatedly, moving from reading to meditation, prayer and contemplation.
sources.application: Small units have a long devotional use; support repetition and pause rather than speed.
sources.limits: A description of practice, not a study.

sources.title: Understanding SC 2.2.2: Pause, Stop, Hide
sources.author: W3C
sources.shows: Anything that moves or auto-updates for more than five seconds alongside other content needs a way to pause, stop or hide it.
sources.application: Auto-advancing verses, read-along and one-word display all need a visible pause.
sources.limits: A Level A criterion for web content; apply the same intent in native apps.

sources.title: Understanding SC 1.4.8: Visual Presentation
sources.author: W3C
sources.shows: Readers should be able to get lines of no more than 80 characters, at least 1.5 line spacing, unjustified text and resizing to 200% without horizontal scrolling.
sources.application: Set reading measure, spacing and size as defaults or reader settings.
sources.limits: Level AAA; a strong target rather than a minimum.

sources.title: Focus Mode
sources.author: iA Writer
sources.shows: Sentence and paragraph focus highlight the active text and dim the rest.
sources.application: A borrowed model for focus with context visible.
sources.limits: A writing tool; the reader’s situation differs.

sources.title: Use Line focus in Immersive Reader
sources.author: Microsoft
sources.shows: Highlights one, three or five lines at a time; presented as helping readers with dyslexia, attention difficulties or visual stress.
sources.application: Offer the size of the focus window as a reader setting.
sources.limits: Vendor documentation, not an outcome study.

sources.title: Effects of highlighting text on the reading ability of children with developmental dyslexia: a pilot study
sources.author: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning
sources.shows: Children with dyslexia found it easier to read along when audio was synchronised with highlighting, especially with whole-sentence highlighting.
sources.application: Move the focus with audio, at the level of a verse or sentence.
sources.limits: Small pilot study.

sources.title: Same language subtitling
sources.author: World Bank blog on Brij Kothari’s work
sources.shows: Karaoke-style same-language subtitles on song programmes in India were associated with gains in reading among early readers.
sources.application: Synchronised text and audio can build reading as a by-product of listening.
sources.limits: Reported programme results; a literacy setting, not Scripture reading.

sources.title: Amazon’s tool for reading, one word at a time
sources.author: VOA Learning English
sources.shows: Kindle Word Runner showed one word at a time at 100–900 words per minute and reported speed at the end of each chapter.
sources.application: A mainstream example of single-word display, and of turning reading into a speed score.
sources.limits: Feature report from 2015; availability may have changed.

sources.title: Maryanne Wolf: building deep reading skills in a digital world
sources.author: UCLA Center for Dyslexia, Diverse Learners, and Social Justice
sources.shows: Wolf argues skimming habits weaken the slower processes of deep reading, and that readers can learn to switch deliberately between modes.
sources.application: Make the slower mode easy to enter and protect it from interruption.
sources.limits: An argument drawing on neuroscience, not a controlled trial of interfaces.

sources.title: dewfall: Bible study and prayer journal
sources.author: Tejas Kumar · App Store listing, version 1.2.0
sources.shows: The listing describes a progress map of all 66 books with “verses read”, streaks and a reading rhythm; in the app each verse can be ticked off as read.
sources.application: Counting by the verse makes the verse the unit of record and splits the text into rows; keep the tick deliberate and separate from opening.
sources.limits: A small, recent app with few ratings; one example of a pattern, not evidence of its effects.

sources.title: Design and the digital Bible: persuasive technology and religious reading
sources.author: Tim Hutchings · Journal of Contemporary Religion 32(2), 2017
sources.shows: Analyses YouVersion and GloBible as persuasive technologies designed to train evangelical reading habits.
sources.application: Ask what reading habit each mode trains, not only whether it is used.
sources.limits: Design analysis of two apps; not a study of readers.
